newsitem.title: USA: Fed rate hike may fail to fire up dollar/yen rally.
newsitem.headline: Fed rate hike may fail to fire up dollar/yen rally.

text.p: Another interest rate hike from the Federal Reserve this month may fail to spur the dollar to new heights versus the yen since many traders would view the move as the last tightening for quite some time, experts said.
Furthermore, some market mavens who aim to stay a step ahead of the game are increasingly weighing the possibility that rock-bottom Japanese rates will eventually head higher.
"I think that the exchange rate reflects expected interest rates rather than actual interest rates," said Takanobu Igarashi, a senior economist at Sanwa Bank Ltd in New York.
If the Fed hikes interest rates on May 20, the majority of the market expects no further increase, at least not in July and August, Igarashi said.
But market players in Japan now expect higher interest rates, especially in the Japanese government bond (JGB) market, he said.

"So, under (these) circumstances, I think that once the Fed hikes interest rates, the dollar will hit its ceiling and may dip somewhat because the rate hike was the last good news for the dollar," Igarashi said.
Fed policymakers next meet on May 20. They had voted to raise the federal funds rate by 25 basis points to 5.50 percent on March 25, the first hike in more than two years.

By contrast, the official Japanese discount rate remains at a record low 0.5 percent. Much of the good news for the dollar has stemmed from such gaping interest rate differentials between Japan and the United States.
But that may change. An article in Japanese financial daily Nikkei Kinyu on Friday speculated on the possibility that Japan's official discount rate may be raised in July.
The Nikkei Kinyu article said some officials in the Bank of Japan (BOJ) may think Japan's low interest rate policy should come to an end soon.
In reaction to the piece, the yield on the benchmark 10-year government bond rose as high as 2.680 percent, up from 2.510 percent at Thursday's close.

"If the Japanese were also in a position to raise rates or the market thought they might be, that move would dominate the Fed's move," said Michael Faust, global portfolio manager at Bailard, Biehl and Kaiser, which manages $350 million in fixed-income securities.

Of course, even if the BOJ did ratchet up official rates by 50 basis points, the interest rate differential between Japan and the United States would still be huge enough that it should continue to underpin the U.S. currency.

"What I think will continue to provide support (for) the currency, even though we saw a major break the last couple of days, ... is the very substantial interest rate differential that we have between here and the rest of the world," said Dimitri Balatsos, president of Tesseract Partners Inc, a global investment advisory firm.
He said that differential will likely began to narrow.
Still, Balatsos said he does not expect a precipitous drop in the dollar but a "stepwise" reduction.
Balatsos said he expects the dollar to trade around 110 yen by year end.
On Friday, a battered dollar tumbled briefly below the key 120 yen threshold to its lowest point since January 27.
At 1400 EDT/1800 GMT, the dollar fetched 120.20/30 yen, down sharply from 121.95/00 at the open.
